goal.title: Learn indoor plant propagation by stem cuttings
goal.focusAreas: Choosing viable stem material; preparing cuttings; managing rooting moisture, drainage, humidity and light; recognizing species differences; deciding when to pot rooted cuttings

sourceDocuments.name: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach: How to Propagate Houseplants by Stem Tip Cuttings
sourceDocuments.text: Source: https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/how-propagate-houseplants-stem-tip-cuttings (accessed 2026-09-06). Paraphrased guidance: The guide recommends 3–6 inch stems with at least two nodes. Remove lower leaves; place at least one node in premoistened rooting medium with leaves above it. Containers need drainage; the medium needs both moisture retention and aeration. Unrooted cuttings lose water while having little capacity to replace it. A loose clear cover can raise humidity; keep it off foliage and allow air exchange. Use bright indirect light: excessive light can burn foliage, particularly under covers. Check conditions regularly and moisten drying medium. Rooting hormone is optional. These are preparation and care recommendations, not a guarantee that every cutting roots.

sourceDocuments.name: University of Minnesota Extension: Monstera deliciosa
sourceDocuments.text: Source: https://extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/propagating-monstera-deliciosa (accessed 2026-09-06). Paraphrased guidance: Monstera deliciosa stem propagation requires a node with an axillary bud. A detached leaf and petiole lacking this stem tissue will not form a new growing plant. A node-bearing cutting can root in several media, including water, so no single medium is necessary. Rooting medium must drain well; excessive wetness and cool soil can lead to disease. Inspect roots gently before moving a cutting; if roots are absent or sparse, return it to the medium. Added auxin may promote rooting, but Monstera can root without it. These statements concern Monstera deliciosa, not every houseplant.

sourceDocuments.name: University of Illinois Extension: Cuttings
sourceDocuments.text: Source: https://extension.illinois.edu/houseplants/cuttings (accessed 2026-09-06). Paraphrased guidance: Illinois recommends starting with insect- and disease-free material. Stem-cutting instructions generally remove leaves below the medium and remove flowers or seeds. Immediate insertion has species exceptions: the article lists some succulents, cacti, Pelargonium and rubber plant as requiring the cut surface to dry and heal first. It describes bright light without direct sun. Rooting speed varies with species and stem characteristics, so its approximate times are not a universal deadline. Check actual roots before potting individually; its guide uses roots about one inch long. Leaf propagation is a different technique that works for some species and cannot be assumed to work for all stem-cutting subjects.

adjudication_checklist.fact: Use moist, aerated medium and containers with drainage.
Bury a node; keep leaves above the medium.
A loose cover raises humidity while allowing air exchange.
Excessive light can burn covered cuttings.
Monstera leaf-and-petiole material alone lacks the required growth point.
Monstera can root in water or solid media.
Sparse roots warrant continued rooting before transfer.
Added auxin is optional for Monstera.
Choose material without insects or disease.
The listed species exceptions need wound drying before insertion.
Rooting speed varies; observe roots before potting.
Leaf-cutting suitability depends on the plant.

goal.title: Learn accessible web forms
goal.focusAreas: visible form labels, explicit label associations, input instructions, identifying form errors

sourceDocuments.name: W3C WAI: Labeling Controls
sourceDocuments.text:
Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/

Labels identify a control's purpose. Associate a label with its control so assistive technology can present that relationship. An explicit HTML label uses a for attribute whose value exactly matches the control's id. Wrapping a control inside its label is another association method. Visible labels help users understand forms. In some layouts the purpose is already clear visually; a visually hidden label can still provide the programmatic label. aria-label supplies an accessible name but does not itself display label text. These alternatives do not mean visible cues are unnecessary in every form.

sourceDocuments.name: W3C WCAG 2.2: Labels or Instructions
sourceDocuments.text:
Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/labels-or-instructions.html

Success Criterion 3.3.2 applies to optional as well as required input fields. Users need labels or instructions indicating what to enter or select. Explain unusual formats or constraints when needed, without unnecessary detail. A label is presented to users; an accessible name may be exposed only through assistive technology. An aria-label alone can provide a programmatic name while leaving other users without the needed visible cue. This criterion is distinct from programmatic association under 1.3.1 and accessible names under 4.1.2. It does not demand a separate visible text label where another adequate label or instruction already communicates the purpose.

sourceDocuments.name: W3C WCAG 2.2: Error Identification
sourceDocuments.text:
Source: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html

Under Success Criterion 3.3.1, automatically detected input errors need text identifying the affected item and describing what is wrong. Missing required input and disallowed formats or values are input errors. Redisplaying a failed form without an error indication is insufficient. Color may supplement the text; color alone does not supply that description. This criterion does not prescribe one layout: messages can appear beside fields, in a summary, or in another suitable presentation. Explaining how to correct an error is addressed separately by 3.3.3, although one message may do both.

adjudication_checklist.check: An explicit label uses the control id as its for value; nearby text alone does not establish this HTML association.
Wrapping a control in a label is possible; explicit association is not the only labeling method.
Hidden labels need context that already communicates purpose visually; do not prescribe hiding every label.
Optional fields also need suitable labels or instructions; required does not limit the criterion to mandatory fields.
A programmatic accessible name alone does not guarantee that all users receive needed labels or instructions.
Explain unfamiliar format constraints when needed; not every simple field needs extra instructions.
For an automatically detected error, identify its field and describe the error in text; color can supplement this.
SC 3.3.1 does not mandate inline errors or a summary; error identification and correction suggestions are distinct.
